power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.title: The Role of Menstrual Cycle Phase and/or Hormonal Fluctuations in PTSD: A Scoping Review of Symptom Expression and Psychotherapy Response in Women
table.type_of_review: This scoping review will be conducted in accordance with the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis (Aromataris et al., 2024), and will be reported according to the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines (Peters et al., 2020; Tricco et al., 2018).
table.review_stages: Search, Pilot Screening, Title/Abstract Screening, Data Extraction, Synthesis, Reporting
table.description:
In Australia, women are diagnosed with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) at approximately twice the rate of men (AIWH, 2025). While this disparity is partly explained by sex-specific trauma exposure patterns, such as differences in trauma type and developmental timing (Eder-Moreau et al., 2022), these factors alone do not fully account for the elevated risk. Furthermore, gold-standard exposure-based psychotherapies for PTSD are only partially effective, with up to 70% of treated individuals relapsing within one year (Schottenbauer et al., 2008). A central challenge in improving treatment outcomes lies in understanding the sex-specific biological and contextual factors that shape symptom expression and the mechanisms underpinning psychotherapies, such as fear extinction learning.
Fluctuations in the female neuroendocrine system have been linked to PTSD vulnerability and symptom severity. Ovarian hormones, particularly oestradiol (E2) and progesterone, have been implicated as robust modulators of PTSD symptoms and outcomes (Ravi et al., 2019). For example, women with PTSD report heightened fear-related and avoidance symptoms during the late luteal/early follicular phases (i.e., low E2 and progesterone) compared to the early- to mid-luteal phases (i.e., higher E2 and progesterone; Nillni et al. (2015)). There is also evidence that the menstrual cycle affects learning and memory. For example, women under stress with high E2 levels (during late follicular phase) demonstrate better declarative memory learning and consolidation compared to women with low E2 levels (during early follicular phase; Antov and Stockhorst (2018)). Furthermore, women using oral contraceptives, which induce tonically low E2 levels, exhibit extinction memory deficits (Graham & Milad, 2013). Additional studies also show that women have enhanced extinction recall if they train when E2 levels are elevated (Kida, 2023). Despite this evidence, the menstrual cycle remains an overlooked factor in PTSD treatment.  Given that fear extinction underpins exposure therapy, these early findings suggest that tailoring psychotherapeutic intervention to menstrual cycle phase could improve outcomes for women.
However, despite promising preliminary findings, there is evidence that the impact of menstrual phase on extinction retention may differ according to PTSD status. For instance, while low E2 is linked to higher PTSD symptoms and impaired threat extinction (Glover et al., 2012), women with PTSD have also shown impaired retention of extinction learning in the mid-luteal menstrual phase (i.e., when E2 and progesterone levels are high), which is an opposite pattern to observations in trauma‐exposed women without PTSD (Pineles et al., 2016). These discrepancies highlight the need to clarify how menstrual-related hormonal factors influence symptomatology and psychological processes specifically in woman with a formal PTSD diagnosis. Moreover, the extent to which laboratory findings have been translated into clinical practice, such as timing treatment delivery to hormonal phases or testing hormonal adjuncts, remains unclear.
To date, no comprehensive review has systematically mapped the literature examining menstrual cycle phase or ovarian hormone levels in relation to i) PTSD symptoms, ii) psychological processes and iii) psychotherapeutic treatment outcomes in woman with a formal PTSD diagnosis. It also remains unclear if and how emerging biological evidence has been operationalised in treatment design or delivery. Given the early stage and multidisciplinary nature of this research, a scoping review is the most suitable approach. By synthesising what is known and what remains to be understood, this review will inform future research directions and support the development of sex-specific, hormone-informed interventions for women with PTSD.
table.research_questions: The primary objective of this scoping review is to map what is known about the influence of menstrual cycle phase and/or ovarian hormonal status on PTSD symptoms and/or related psychological processes in females. Specifically, we aim to map and synthesise research examining how menstrual cycle phase and/or endogenous or exogenous ovarian hormones (e.g., estrogen, progesterone) impact the expression, severity, or fluctuation of PTSD symptoms and related psychological processes (e.g., extinction learning) in females (Aim 1). not applicable
table.secondary_research_question_s:
The secondary objective is to examine whether these menstrual-related factors influence psychotherapy outcomes in PTSD and related anxiety disorders, and to determine the extent to which this association has been explicitly studied. Specifically, we aim to explore whether menstrual cycle phase or hormonal status influences the efficacy or outcomes of psychological therapies for PTSD and other anxiety-related disorders, such as generalised anxiety disorder, panic disorder and phobias (Aim 2).

Additionally, we aim to:
•	Detail how menstrual cycle phase, hormonal status, PTSD symptoms, and therapy/treatment outcomes have been defined and measured across included studies.
•	Identify key knowledge gaps and methodological limitations to inform future research and clinical practice.

table.data_exclusion_criteria:
This review will be guided by the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework recommended by the JBI (Aromataris et al., 2024). We will include empirical studies involving females (Population), that examine the impact of menstrual cycle phase and/or hormonal status on i) PTSD symptoms or related processes, or ii) psychotherapy response in PTSD or other anxiety-related disorders (Concept), in any setting or context (Context). These criteria are described in detail below.

Participants
Eligible studies must include biological females with:
•	A PTSD diagnosis and assessment of menstrual cycle phase and/or ovarian hormones in relation to PTSD symptomatology or related psychological processes (Aim 1), or
•	A diagnosis of PTSD or a related anxiety disorder with assessment of psychotherapy outcomes in relation to menstrual cycle phase and/or ovarian hormones (Aim 2).
Studies will be included if they:
•	Provide an explicit measurement of ovarian hormones or menstrual cycle phase (via biological assay or self-report).
•	Report on females who are:
o	naturally cycling,
o	using hormonal contraceptives, or
o	in or beyond the menopause transition, provided hormonal status or cycle phase is measured.
Studies will be excluded if they:
•	Include females aged <18 years,
•	Do not include a PTSD sample (Aim 1) or a PTSD/anxiety disorder sample (Aim 2),
•	Are male-only samples, or
•	Involve animal subjects.
Due to the scoping nature of this review, no strict upper age limits will be applied; however, findings will be interpreted in the context of age-related factors (e.g., menopause transition).

Concept
This review will focus on the influence of menstrual cycle phase and/or ovarian hormone status on:
•	PTSD-related symptoms (e.g., severity, fluctuations), or
•	Psychological processes relevant to PTSD (e.g., extinction learning, extinction retention, memory reconsolidation), or 
•	Treatment outcomes (response or efficacy for PTSD or anxiety-related disorders).
Studies that do not include females with PTSD (Aim 1) or anxiety-related disorder (Aim 2), do not explicitly measure menstrual cycle phase or hormonal status, or do not assess any of the above criteria will be excluded.

Context
Only peer-reviewed studies published in English will be included. There will be no restriction on geographic location, cultural setting, or study environment. Studies may be conducted in clinical, laboratory, academic, or community-based contexts, provided they meet the eligibility criteria detailed in this protocol.

Types of sources
This review will consider a broad range of empirical study designs, including both quantitative and qualitative research, as well as cross-sectional and longitudinal trials.
Quantitative study designs may include:
•	Experimental and quasi-experimental studies, such as randomised controlled trials, non-randomised controlled trials, and time-series, as well as 
•	Analytical observational studies, including prospective and retrospective cohort studies, case-control studies/case series, and analytical cross-sectional studies.
Qualitative studies will be included if they examine experiences or processes relevant to PTSD symptoms or psychotherapy in the context of menstrual cycle phase or hormonal fluctuations, provided that these hormonal factors are measured or explicitly considered (e.g., via self-report).
The following sources will be excluded:
•	Review papers (including narrative, conceptual, systematic, or scoping),
•	Book chapters,
•	Study protocols,
•	Theses,
•	Editorials or commentaries, and
•	Conference abstracts.

table.search_strategy_justification:
Our search strategy balances comprehensiveness with feasibility. We selected six major databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, ProQuest) to cover medical, psychological, and interdisciplinary literature relevant to PTSD, menstrual cycle, and hormonal factors. Two complementary search strings were developed to capture both symptom expression and psychotherapy outcomes, with terms iteratively refined through a structured two-step approach.

Grey literature was not included to maintain focus on peer-reviewed empirical studies, ensuring quality and replicability. Authors will be contacted only when critical information is missing or unclear, with communications documented while protecting personal data. The search will be conducted and updated prior to publication to ensure inclusion of the most current studies. This strategy ensures scientific rigor while remaining practical and manageable within the scope of the review.
table.screening_stages:
Initially, a structured two-step approach was used to develop a comprehensive and replicable search strategy. First, a limited search of PubMed and PsycINFO was undertaken to identify relevant articles and refine the search terms. Titles, abstracts, and index terms of relevant studies were examined to identify keywords and text words commonly used in the literature. The second step involved using the results of the initial search to develop two complementary search strategies designed to address the review’s dual focus: (1) the relationship between menstrual cycle/ovarian hormonal factors and PTSD symptom expression/psychological processes in PTSD samples, and (2) the influence of these factors on psychotherapy outcomes in PTSD and anxiety-related disorders. While the core structure of the search remained consistent, minor adaptations were made for each database to account for specific syntax or indexing differences (e.g., truncation discrepancies, term limits). Following the literature search, all references will be exported to EndNote and then imported into Covidence for de-duplication as well as management of the screening and data extraction processes. Prior to formal screening, a pilot exercise will be conducted on the first 30 entries by two independent reviewers to i) ensure consistent application of the inclusion criteria, and ii) resolve any discrepancies regarding eligibility criteria before continuing. 
Once high consistency is achieved across reviewers (>90% agreement), the reviewers will proceed to screen all titles and abstracts independently in accordance with the outlined eligibility criteria. Upon completion of title/abstract screening, the reference lists of included studies will be manually examined to identify any relevant literature that may have been missed. Similarly, any relevant reviews, protocols, or commentaries identified during the search will be scanned for eligible empirical studies. All potentially relevant articles will then be retrieved in full and assessed for eligibility based on the pre-established inclusion and exclusion criteria by two independent reviewers. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage will be documented. Disagreements at any stage will be resolved by consensus, or if needed, adjudicated by a third independent reviewer.
table.screened_fields_blinding: During title/abstract and full-text screening in Covidence, all bibliographic fields (e.g., title, abstract, authors, journal, DOI and year) will be visible to reviewers
table.used_exclusion_criteria:
Studies will be excluded if they:
•	Do not include biological women with a PTSD diagnosis and assessment of menstrual cycle phase and/or ovarian hormones in relation to PTSD symptomatology or related psychological processes (Aim 1),
•	Do not include biological women with a diagnosis of PTSD or a related anxiety disorder with assessment of psychotherapy outcomes in relation to menstrual cycle phase and/or ovarian hormones (Aim 2).
•      Do not include explicit measurement of ovarian hormones or menstrual cycle phase (via self-report or biological assay, for instance),
•	Include females aged <18 years,
•	Do not include a PTSD sample (Aim 1) or a PTSD/anxiety disorder sample (Aim 2),
•	Are male-only samples, 
•	Are not published,
•	Are not available in English, 
•	They are a review paper, book chapter, study protocol, thesis, editorial/commentary, conference abstract, or
•	Involve only animal subjects.
table.screener_instructions:
Screening will be conducted in Covidence. Two independent reviewers will screen all titles/abstracts and full texts against the predefined eligibility criteria (Population–Concept–Context framework). A pilot screening of the first 30 references will be completed to ensure consistent application of the criteria (>90% agreement) before continuing.

At the title/abstract stage, studies will be included if potentially relevant; exclusion requires clear ineligibility. At the full-text stage, inclusion/exclusion decisions will be made according to the eligibility criteria (population, concept, context, study type), and reasons for exclusion will be recorded. Disagreements will be resolved through discussion, or by a third reviewer if required.

The full set of eligibility criteria and decision rules is detailed in the protocol uploaded to this OSF project.
table.screening_reliability: Two independent reviewers will conduct both title/abstract and full-text screening in Covidence. A pilot test of the first 30 references will be undertaken to ensure consistent application of eligibility criteria, with >90% agreement required before proceeding. Screening will then be conducted independently. Disagreements resolved by discussion or, if needed, adjudication by a third reviewer. Agreement will be assessed during the pilot phase and monitored throughout the process.
table.screening_reconciliation_procedure: Disagreements resolved by discussion or, if needed, adjudication by a third reviewer. Agreement will be assessed during the pilot phase and monitored throughout the process.
table.sample_size: As this is a scoping review, all studies meeting the inclusion criteria will be included; no sampling will be applied. The aim is to map the scope, nature, and characteristics of existing research rather than test hypotheses requiring power calculations. Consequently, no minimum sample size or power analysis is applicable.
table.screening_procedure_justification: Dual independent screening at both title/abstract and full-text levels increases reliability and reduces bias, while a pilot round ensures consistent application of inclusion/exclusion criteria. Blinding of bibliographic fields (e.g., authors, journal) was not implemented, as the risk of bias at this stage is minimal and full visibility supports accurate eligibility decisions. Inclusion/exclusion criteria are explicitly defined according to the PCC framework to ensure transparency and replicability. Disagreements are reconciled through discussion or adjudication by a third reviewer, which provides quality assurance while remaining practical for the review’s scope.
table.data_management_and_sharing: Database search results will be exported in RIS format to Endnote (exported from EndNote to covidence in XML format) and data extraction and screening decisions will be shared in CSV/XLSX format. No embargo is planned. All extracted data will be recorded in Excel data charting files (XLSX). These files will be uploaded to the project’s OSF repository to ensure transparency and reproducibility. No embargo is planned; files will be publicly accessible once the review is completed.
table.entities_to_extract: From each included study we will extract the following: bibliographic metadata (title, author(s), year of publication, citation details); study characteristics (aim, context, and method); and sample characteristics (sample description, sample size, mean age, menstruation status, inclusion and exclusion criteria). We will also extract details of menstrual cycle or hormonal assessment methods and grouping approaches (e.g., cycle phase, contraceptive use, menopausal status). For outcomes, we will capture PTSD  symptoms, relevant psychological processes (e.g., extinction learning), diagnostic groups assessed, and any treatment/intervention type and outcome measures. Finally, we will extract a summary of the reported hormonal or menstrual effects. This process of extracting characteristics and dimensions will be continuously updated through an interactive approach, with refinements made as needed to ensure all relevant information is captured consistently across studies. Any modifications will be explicitly reported.
table.extraction_stages: Data extraction will be conducted in several stages. First, a training stage will be undertaken in which two reviewers independently pilot the extraction forms on a small number of included studies to ensure clarity, consistency, and alignment with the review objectives. Second, during the main extraction stage, two reviewers will independently extract data in parallel from all included studies using the predefined extraction tables. Discrepancies will be discussed and resolved by consensus, with a third reviewer available to adjudicate if needed. Third, a reliability verification stage will be performed by cross-checking the completed tables to ensure accuracy and completeness of extracted entities. All extraction will be conducted manually by humans, using Microsoft Excel forms, with no use of AI or automated extraction tools. The extraction process will remain iterative, with refinements to the charting forms and procedures documented transparently.
table.extractor_instructions:
Extractors will follow a structured protocol to ensure consistency. For each included study, they will:
Record bibliographic and study characteristics (aim, context, method).
Capture sample details (size, age, menstruation status, inclusion/exclusion criteria).
Note menstrual/hormonal assessment methods and participant grouping.
Extract PTSD/anxiety outcomes and any treatment/intervention effects.
Summarise reported hormonal or menstrual effects.
Enter data into the standardised Excel extraction tables (Data Extraction Tables.xlsx, OSF project).
Flag uncertainties for discussion with a second extractor; reach consensus before finalising.
Document any form adaptations.
table.extraction_reliability:
Data from included studies will be independently extracted by two reviewers using standardised charting forms in Microsoft Excel. Each extractor will independently complete the extraction for all included studies. Discrepancies between extractors will be identified and discussed; if consensus cannot be reached, a third reviewer will adjudicate.

To assess extraction reliability, we will calculate inter-rater agreement (e.g., percentage agreement) on a subset of studies during the pilot extraction phase. High consistency (>90% agreement) will be confirmed before proceeding to full extraction. Any modifications or refinements to extraction procedures will be documented.
table.extraction_reconciliation_procedure: To assess extraction reliability, we will calculate inter-rater agreement (e.g., percentage agreement) on a subset of studies during the pilot extraction phase. High consistency (>90% agreement) will be confirmed before proceeding to full extraction. Any modifications or refinements to extraction procedures will be documented.
table.extraction_procedure_justification:
Extraction procedures were designed to balance rigour and feasibility. Two independent extractors will ensure reliable capture of all relevant study information, including bibliographic metadata, sample characteristics, hormonal/menstrual measures, PTSD/anxiety outcomes, and treatment effects. The use of standardised Excel charting forms and a data dictionary supports consistency.

Pilot testing on a subset of studies will identify ambiguities and refine extraction procedures, ensuring high inter-rater reliability (>90% agreement) before full extraction. Discrepancies will be resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer adjudicating unresolved cases, which preserves data accuracy without excessive burden.

All extraction decisions, refinements to forms, and reconciliation procedures will be documented to maintain transparency and reproducibility, while allowing for iterative improvement of the extraction process.
table.transformations: Quantitative outcomes will be standardised where appropriate (e.g., effect sizes may be converted to Cohen’s d or Pearson’s r) for comparability across studies. Categorical or qualitative data (e.g., menstrual phase, contraceptive type, therapy type) will be recoded into predefined categories (e.g., menstruation, follicular, ovulation, luteal) All transformations will be documented, with raw data retained, ensuring transparency and alignment with the review’s variables of interest.

table.synthesis_reliability: The data synthesis will be conducted by one primary synthesist. To ensure reliability, key decisions  and interpretations will be reviewed and discussed with a second team member. Discrepancies or uncertainties will be resolved through consensus, and any revisions will be documented.

table.synthesis_procedure_justification: Synthesis balances rigour and feasibility. Quantitative data will be standardised and qualitative data recoded. Data integrity is ensured via prior independent extraction, with discrepancies discussed and missing/ambiguous data flagged. One primary synthesist will conduct the synthesis, with all interpretations reviewed by a second team member. Conclusions will be based on consistent reporting of hormonal measures, PTSD/anxiety outcomes, and treatment effects, and all decisions will be documented. text.text: Women are diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) at twice the rate of men, a disparity only partly explained by trauma exposure differences.

Sex-specific biological factors, particularly cyclic fluctuations in estradiol and progesterone, have been associated with PTSD symptoms/related neuropsychological processes in healthy/trauma exposed women; however, the extent and clinical translation of this literature (if any) remain unclear in PTSD populations.

This review aimed to map evidence examining associations between ovarian hormones/menstrual cycle phase and PTSD symptoms and/or related neuropsychological processes (e.g., extinction learning) in women with PTSD (Aim1), and/or associations with psychotherapy outcomes in PTSD/related anxiety disorders (Aim2).
A systematic search for peer-reviewed, empirical studies involving adult females was conducted across 6 databases, in accordance with PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidelines.
From 2,464 results, 12 studies were included.
Five studies addressed Aim 1 and seven addressed Aim 2.

Hormonal operationalization was inconsistent, including continuous assays (n=5), menstrual cycle phase comparisons (n=3), and/or median split/other groupings (n=6), with estradiol most frequently measured.
For Aim 1, PTSD symptom findings were inconsistent and inconclusive (n=3), whereas lower estradiol was more consistently associated with impaired fear extinction and habituation (n=2).
For Aim 2, findings in anxiety-related disorders were mixed, with no study examining ovarian hormone status in psychotherapy outcomes for women with PTSD.
Overall, evidence remains sparse, heterogeneous and largely cross-sectional.

Findings do not yet support firm conclusions regarding ovarian hormone-PTSD symptom/neuropsychological interactions but highlight key research gaps and future directions to better understand these relationships and inform personalized PTSD treatments for women.
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a debilitating psychiatric condition that can develop following exposure to a traumatic event.

Individuals with PTSD may experience intrusive recollections of the trauma, including sensory nightmares or flashbacks, alongside hypervigilance, sleep disturbance, impaired concentration, irritability, emotional withdrawal, and avoidance behaviors (APA, 2022; Yehuda et al., 2015).

text.text: Thus, optimizing the timing of existing interventions according to menstrual cycle phase or ovarian hormone status, or indeed utilizing hormonal adjuncts (Hammoud et al., 2020), may therefore represent a promising precision medicine approach to improve PTSD treatment outcomes for women.

text.text: However, despite increasing interest in this concept (Bolea-Alamanac et al., 2018; Glover et al., 2015; Tang & Graham, 2020), the extent to which menstrual cycle phase or ovarian hormone status influences PTSD symptom expression, neuropsychological processes, and psychotherapy outcomes remains unclear in clinical populations.

text.text: In healthy/trauma-exposed populations, when considering learning and memory processes relevant to PTSD and its treatment, hormones such as E2 have been shown to play an important role.

For instance, correlational studies demonstrate that higher E2 levels are associated with enhanced declarative memory learning and consolidation under high stress (Antov & Stockhorst, 2018), threat/fear conditioning and extinction learning (Hammoud et al., 2020), as well as extinction recall (Kida, 2023).

text.text: Animal models provide further evidence that E2 is a biological modulator of extinction-related learning processes.

For example, in female rodents, endogenous fluctuations in ovarian hormones across the estrous cycle influence conditioned fear extinction, with elevated hormone states associated with enhanced extinction learning and recall (Milad et al., 2009).

text.text: Importantly though, despite this preclinical evidence, findings from clinical human populations appear more complex.

While lower E2 and/or P4 levels have been associated with poorer emotional memory consolidation and extinction recall in healthy women (Hsu et al., 2021), women with PTSD have demonstrated impaired retention of extinction learning during the mid-luteal menstrual phase, when E2 and P4 levels are typically elevated (Pineles et al., 2016).

text.text: These discrepancies suggest that ovarian hormone influences on related neuropsychological processes may differ between healthy and PTSD populations, highlighting the importance of examining associations stratified by PTSD status.

This evidence also has important potential implications for psychotherapy, particularly exposure-based interventions that rely on extinction learning processes (Knowles & Tolin, 2022; Sep et al., 2023).

text.text: That said, it remains unclear if and how emerging biological evidence has been operationalized in treatment design or delivery.

To date, no review has systematically mapped the literature examining menstrual cycle phase or ovarian hormone status in relation to PTSD symptoms, related neuropsychological processes, and psychotherapy outcomes in women with a PTSD diagnosis.
Given the early-stage and multidisciplinary nature of this research area, a scoping review was deemed the most appropriate approach.

The primary objective of this scoping review was to map and synthesize research in women with a formal PTSD diagnosis examining the relationship between menstrual cycle phase and/or ovarian hormone status and a) PTSD symptom expression, severity, or fluctuation (Aim 1a), or b) neuropsychological processes relevant to PTSD, such as extinction learning, extinction retention, and memory reconsolidation (Aim 1b).

A secondary objective was to examine whether menstrual cycle phase or ovarian hormonal status influences psychotherapy outcomes in PTSD or related anxiety disorders, such as panic disorder and phobia (Aim 2).

In doing so, we detail the extent of this literature, and how menstrual cycle phase, hormonal status, PTSD symptoms, and therapy/treatment outcomes have been measured across included studies, whilst identifying key gaps within the current literature.

This synthesis provides a systematic overview of the scope and nature of research in this emerging field, and highlights directions for future hormone-informed PTSD research and the downstream implications for treatment.

text.text: To identify potentially relevant studies, a systematic search of the following six electronic databases was performed in August 2025: PUBMED, Scopus, Web of Science, Medline (Ovid), PsychINFO, and ProQuest (One Academic).
The final search strategy was initially developed using a structured two-step approach.
First, a limited search of PubMed and PsycINFO was undertaken to identify relevant articles and refine the search terms.
Titles, abstracts, and index terms of relevant studies were examined to identify keywords and text words commonly used in the literature.
The second step involved using the results of the initial search to develop two complementary search strategies designed to address the review's dual focus.
To validate the strategy, a set of key known relevant articles were identified, and the search was tested to ensure these articles were retrieved.

While the core structure of the search remained consistent, minor adaptations were made for each database to account for specific syntax or indexing differences (e.g., truncation discrepancies, term limits).
An experienced academic librarian was also consulted on the search strategy before implementation.

text.text: In addition to database searching, we also conducted backward citation tracking and checked the reference list of related sources (e.g., reviews, protocols, or commentaries) discovered during the search process.

Nine corresponding authors were contacted seeking additional data.

One responded supplying the requested data, two revealed that the requested data was published elsewhere (both publications were already captured in the search), three replied that the requested analyses were not available, and three did not respond to email enquiry.

Upon completion of the literature search, all references were exported from respective databases into EndNote and then imported into Covidence for de-duplication as well as management of the screening processes.

Prior to formal screening, a pilot exercise was conducted on the first 30 entries by two independent reviewers (C.T and K.M) to ensure consistent application of the inclusion criteria and resolve any discrepancies regarding eligibility criteria before continuing.
Once high consistency was achieved across reviewers (> 90% agreement), we proceeded to screen all titles and abstracts independently in accordance with the outlined eligibility criteria.

text.text: All potentially relevant articles were then retrieved in full and assessed for eligibility based on the pre-established inclusion and exclusion criteria by two independent reviewers (C.T and K.M).
Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were documented.
Disagreements at any stage were resolved by consensus, or if needed, adjudicated by a third independent reviewer (A.B).
Peer-reviewed empirical studies were included if they were, published in English, included females with either a i.

PTSD diagnosis and assessment of menstrual cycle phase and/or ovarian hormones in relation to PTSD symptomatology (Aim 1a) or related neuropsychological processes such as extinction learning, extinction retention, or memory reconsolidation (Aim 1b), or ii. diagnosis of PTSD or a related anxiety disorder with assessment of psychotherapy outcomes in relation to menstrual cycle phase and/or ovarian hormones (Aim 2).

Studies were included if they provided an explicit measurement of ovarian hormones or menstrual cycle phase (via biological assay or self-report), reported on females (naturally cycling, using hormonal contraceptives, or in or beyond the menopause transition, provided hormonal status or cycle phase was measured).
Studies were excluded if they involved females aged < 18 years, did not include a PTSD sample (Aim 1) or a PTSD/anxiety disorder sample (Aim 2), male-only samples, or only animal subjects.

This scoping review mapped the available evidence examining associations between menstrual cycle phase and/or ovarian hormone status and PTSD symptom expression, related neuropsychological processes, and psychotherapy outcomes in women with PTSD.

Despite growing interest in the role of the menstrual cycle/ovarian hormones in the context of PTSD (Green & Graham, 2022; Nillni et al., 2021; Peltier et al., 2024), only 12 studies met our inclusion criteria, highlighting the limited evidence available in clinically diagnosed PTSD populations.

text.text: Indeed, much of the broader evidence base has focused on healthy/trauma-exposed populations, providing important mechanistic insights but nonetheless limiting conclusions regarding clinical presentations.

To summarize, our findings did not support a consistent relationship between ovarian hormones and PTSD symptom severity outcomes in women with PTSD but did suggest that lower E2 concentrations were more consistently associated with impaired fear habituation and extinction-related processes.

Notwithstanding, the clinical significance of these effects remain unclear, especially given that no study to date has empirically tested whether ovarian hormone status or menstrual cycle phase influences psychotherapy outcomes in women with PTSD, particularly with intensive PTSD treatment.

Overall, the findings of this review were derived from a small number of heterogeneous studies employing diverse approaches to outcome measurement/selection, including hormonal assessment and menstrual cycle classification (or lack thereof).

Collectively, the available evidence suggests that ovarian hormones may influence neuropsychological processes that are cardinal to PTSD (e.g., fear extinction), but whether this translates to treatment effectiveness remains elusive.

Evidence examining associations between ovarian hormones and PTSD symptom-level outcomes was limited (Adams et al., 2025; Glover et al., 2012; Nillni et al., 2015) with each study employing different approaches to hormonal assessment, including continuous hormone concentrations, menstrual cycle phase comparisons, and dichotomized hormone groupings.

text.text: Across these studies, findings did not demonstrate a consistent relationship between ovarian hormone status and overall PTSD symptom severity, suggesting that ovarian hormones may not directly influence symptom expression, though firm conclusions cannot be ascertained from such a small sample size.
PTSD is a complex and heterogeneous disorder involving multiple symptom domains, including intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and hyperarousal (APA, 2022).

It is therefore possible that ovarian hormones influence specific symptom dimensions or underlying biological processes rather than overall symptom severity scores, as were employed in the included studies.
Furthermore, all studies examining symptom associations were predominantly cross-sectional, which does little to elucidate temporal change.

It remains unclear whether ovarian hormone variation contributes to PTSD symptom fluctuation, reflects downstream consequences of PTSD-related stress physiology, or interacts with other biological and environmental factors.
Longitudinal studies incorporating repeated hormone measurement and symptom assessment across the menstrual cycle are required to clarify these relationships.

Compared with symptom-level outcomes, more consistent patterns emerged regarding ovarian hormones and neuropsychological processes cardinal to PTSD, particularly fear conditioning, habituation, and extinction.

Across studies employing dichotomized E2 concentrations, lower E2 levels were associated with poorer fear habituation and extinction-related processes among women with PTSD (Glover et al., 2012; Sartin-Tarm et al., 2020).

text.text: However, the current review does not support a straightforward interpretation that higher E2 menstrual states universally enhance fear extinction.
In particular, Pineles et al. (2016) reported poorer extinction retention among women with PTSD during the mid-luteal phase, when both E2 and P4 are typically elevated.

text.text: In contrast, trauma-exposed controls demonstrated poorer extinction retention during the early follicular phase, characterised by lower ovarian hormone concentrations.

Although these phase-based findings suggest that associations between menstrual cycle phase and extinction retention may differ according to PTSD status, they do not necessarily indicate that higher E2 is detrimental to extinction retention in women with PTSD.

Indeed, supplementary analyses examining hormone concentrations as continuous variables revealed that higher P4 was associated with poorer extinction outcomes in the PTSD group, particularly when E2 was also low.
This finding highlights the importance of considering the broader hormonal context rather than interpreting menstrual cycle phase as a proxy for E2 alone.
It may also help reconcile the phase-based findings with evidence that progesterone can oppose oestradiol's facilitative effects on fear extinction in rats (Graham & Daher, 2016).

text.text: This altered pathway could potentially limit the expected anxiolytic and inhibitory effects of P4, particularly during the mid-luteal phase when P4 concentrations increase.

Thus, reduced ALLO availability during the mid luteal phase in PTSD is thereby problematic and may also obscure the hypothesized beneficial effects of higher E2 and P4 concentrations on extinction retention in PTSD, highlighting the importance of considering hormone effects within the broader hormonal and neurobiological milieu of each menstrual cycle phase.
Collectively, these findings suggest that ovarian hormones may represent a biological moderator of PTSD-related learning processes, particularly extinction mechanisms relevant to psychotherapy.
However, further work is required to determine whether laboratory-based hormone-related effects actually translate into clinically meaningful differences in treatment response.
A major gap identified by this review was the absence of studies examining ovarian hormone status or menstrual cycle phase in relation to psychotherapy outcomes among women with PTSD.

This represents an important limitation, since many evidence-based PTSD treatments rely on learning and memory processes, including extinction learning, inhibitory learning, and memory reconsolidation (Knowles & Tolin, 2022; Sep et al., 2023), which were consistently associated with ovarian hormones here, and elsewhere (Hammoud et al., 2020; Kida, 2023).

text.text: Variation in anxiety disorder populations, intervention paradigms, hormone assessment approaches, and follow-up durations further limits comparison between studies, nor are they mutually exclusive.

Therefore, although mechanistic studies provide a rationale for considering ovarian hormones as potential moderators of treatment response, evidence is currently insufficient to support clinical recommendations regarding potential menstrual cycle timing of psychotherapy or hormone-informed PTSD treatment delivery.
A key priority identified by this review is greater methodological consistency in the assessment of ovarian hormones and menstrual cycle phase.

The included studies varied substantially in their use of continuous hormone assays, median-split classifications, menstrual phase comparisons, contraceptivebased comparisons, and pharmacological manipulation (Figure 3), limiting cross-study comparison and making it difficult to determine whether apparently discrepant findings reflect genuine biological differences or methodological variation.

text.text: Future research should therefore prioritize rigorous menstrual cycle characterization using prospective cycle mapping alongside urinary LH testing and, where feasible, serum and/or salivary hormone measurement, rather than relying on retrospective self-reported cycle phase.

Repeated hormone assessment across the menstrual cycle would allow endocrine state to be characterized continuously and in relation to the individual's cycle trajectory, rather than reducing hormone concentrations to arbitrary high-versus low-hormone categories using approaches such as median splits.

Sampling during biologically defined phases (e.g., early follicular versus mid luteal) could additionally facilitate within-person comparisons of relatively low versus high E2 states while accounting for the broader hormonal changes occurring across the cycle.
This approach may also provide a useful framework for investigating whether the timing of psychotherapy relative to E2 state influences treatment response.

Given the potential for PTSD-related alterations in P4-to-ALLO metabolism to influence the interpretation of mid-luteal effects when P4 and E2 increase, an initial focus on the follicular phase may provide a more controlled approach to isolating the potential contribution of E2.

For example, comparing delivery of intensive psychotherapy during early ("low E2") and late ("high E2") follicular phases could therefore help establish whether E2 state influences psychotherapy response before extending this work to other phases of the menstrual cycle.
In any case, a multi-hormone approach will ultimately be important, as E2 cannot be considered independently of the broader hormonal and neurobiological changes occurring across the menstrual cycle.

In order to effectively address the apparent gap in clinical translation, future randomized clinical trials should integrate rigorous menstrual cycle and endocrine assessment with validated PTSD outcomes to determine whether the menstrual cycle contributes to variability in treatment response.

Establishing whether experimental hormone-related effects are reproducible and clinically meaningful will be essential before hormone-informed treatment timing can be considered a viable precision medicine approach for women with PTSD.

This is the first review to map the published empirical evidence to date examining the associations between menstrual cycle phase and/or ovarian hormone status and PTSD symptom expression, PTSDrelated neuropsychological processes, and psychotherapy outcomes in women with a formal PTSD diagnosis.
While the review benefits from a systematic PRISMA-aligned approach, we acknowledge several limitations.
First, although a comprehensive search strategy across six databases was undertaken, the overall evidence base identified was small, with only 12 studies meeting inclusion criteria.
The limited number of eligible studies restricted the ability to draw definitive conclusions regarding the relationship between ovarian hormones, menstrual cycle phase, and PTSD-related outcomes.

Second, substantial heterogeneity existed across included studies in participant characteristics, trauma exposure, diagnostic approaches, hormonal assessment methods, menstrual cycle classification strategies, and outcome measures, further limited direct comparison between studies.

Additionally, many studies relied on single hormone assessments or dichotomized hormone classifications, which may not adequately capture dynamic ovarian hormone fluctuations across the menstrual cycle.
Findings should therefore be interpreted as mapping the current evidence base rather than providing definitive estimates of hormone-related effects.

Third, consistent with the purpose of a scoping review, this review aimed to map the extent and characteristics of available evidence rather than formally evaluate methodological quality or risk of bias.
Although methodological limitations of included studies were discussed, formal critical appraisal was not undertaken.

As this field develops and more rigorous longitudinal and intervention studies become available, systematic reviews and metaanalytic approaches will be required to determine the strength and consistency of observed associations.

This scoping review revealed no consistent relationship between ovarian hormone status and overall PTSD symptom severity but did show that lower E2 was more consistently associated with impaired fear habituation and extinction-related processes, suggesting a potential hormonal influence on neuropsychological mechanisms cardinal to PTSD.

No studies have examined whether menstrual cycle phase or ovarian hormone status influences psychotherapy outcomes in women with PTSD, leaving the clinical significance of these neuropsychological findings unresolved.

Future research should prioritize rigorous, within-person menstrual cycle mapping with repeated multi-hormone assessment to better characterize hormonal trajectories and their relationship with PTSD-related processes.
